<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, here’s how to approach drawing a detailed system design diagram that accurately represents this project’s architecture:

1. Project Overview & Purpose:
   • This repository is a collection of open-source scripts designed to make patching various Android apps (such as YouTube, YouTube Music, Facebook, Twitter, etc.) easier. Users choose from options like “Revanced” or “Revanced Extended” (including beta, stable, and lite variations) and select the appropriate CPU architecture.
   • The core purpose is to simplify the patching process by integrating various external patching projects into a unified, automated script-running system.

2. Identify the Main Components:
   • GitHub CI/CD Integration:
     – The “.github” folder contains actions and workflows. This represents the automated CI/CD pipeline that builds, tests, and releases updated patch files.
   • Build Scripts Engine:
     – The “src/build” directory holds numerous shell scripts for building different variants (e.g., Revanced.sh, Revanced-Extended.sh, and their beta/Android version counterparts). This is where the main build logic lives.
   • Patch & Options Modules:
     – The “src/patches” folder is organized by target apps (YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, etc.). Each app folder contains “include-patches” and “exclude-patches” directories to determine which modifications get applied.
     – The “src/options” folder supplies configuration files (in JSON format) that correspond to specific patching scenarios or app variants.
   • Utility and Environment Configuration Scripts:
     – The “src/etc” folder contains helper scripts (for tasks like managing connections or CI-specific configuration) along with key files like the keystore.
   • Supporting Documentation:
     – The “docs” folder, which contains FAQs and visual assets (banner images), supports user guidance and troubleshooting.

3. Determine Component Relationships and Data Flow:
   • User Input & Configuration:
     – Users start by selecting the target app and variant (from Revanced options) along with appropriate CPU architecture. This decision ties into the “options” JSON files.
   • Build & Patch Generation:
     – The selected options trigger execution of the corresponding build script (located in “src/build”), which in turn refers to the appropriate patches (from “src/patches”) and configuration files.
     – Utility scripts (in “src/etc”) may be called during the build process to manage environment settings, CI integration, or connectivity.
   • CI/CD Pipeline:
     – GitHub Actions (found in “.github/workflows” and inside “.github/actions”) automatically execute build scripts, validate patch integrity, and release new patch builds. The diagram should show CI/CD as a separate but connected component that triggers the build process.
   • External Dependencies:
     – External dependencies like MicroG or other repositories (mentioned in the README) should be represented as external services or libraries that the build process depends on.
      
4. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular design principle: The repository is structured into modular directories (build scripts, patches, options) that separate concerns. Each app’s patches are isolated in their own subdirectories, making extension or maintenance easier.
   • Script-driven automation: The system relies on shell scripts organized clearly by build type, enabling automation and customization.
   • CI/CD integration: Emphasize the automated pipelines (GitHub Actions) that drive testing and release processes.
      
5. Drawing the Diagram – Guidelines for the Principal Software Engineer:
   • Use distinct shapes or colors for each kind of component:
     – GitHub CI/CD: Use a cloud icon or a distinct color block representing “CI/CD Pipeline.” Include elements for “Workflows,” “Actions,” and “Manual Patch/Release.”
     – Build Engine: Represent the “Build Scripts” component (src/build) with a processing block. Label each build script type or group (standard, extended, beta, Android-specific) as sub-components.
     – Patch Repository and Options: Depict these as configuration modules. Use folders or database icons to show “Patches” (src/patches by app) and “Options” (src/options).
     – Utility & Environment: Represent “etc” scripts and keystore files as supporting services feeding into the build process.
     – External Services: Add external dependency icons for projects like ReVanced Patches, MicroG, and integration with third-party tools.
   • Directional arrows:
     – Draw arrows from the “User Configuration/Selection” node to the “Build Scripts” node.
     – Show flow from “Build Scripts” to “Patches” and “Options.”
     – Depict how “CI/CD Pipeline” initiates and monitors the build process.
     – Illustrate feedback or dependency flows (e.g., external libraries feeding into the build process).
   • Clear labeling:
     – Each component should be clearly labelled (e.g., “GitHub Actions CI/CD,” “Build Scripts Engine – src/build,” “App-Specific Patches – src/patches/{app},” “Configuration Options – src/options,” “Utility Scripts – src/etc”).
   • Use directional arrows to indicate:
     – Data/configuration flow (from Options to Build Scripts).
     – Execution control (from CI/CD to Build Scripts).
     – Dependency relationships (Build Scripts relying on Patches and Utility scripts).
     
6. Tailor the Diagram to This Specific Project Type:
   • Since this is a script-driven patching tool for Android apps, focus on the workflow from user selection, through the build process, to the output APK generation.
   • Highlight modularity (separate patch directories) and the multi-variant build support that the repository provides (for different architectures and app variants).
   • Emphasize the integration point with GitHub Actions that drives the update and release cycle.

7. Final Checklist for the Diagram:
   • Include Component Labels: Clearly mark “User Input/Selection,” “Build Scripts Engine,” “App Patches,” “Configuration Options,” “Utility Scripts,” “CI/CD Pipeline,” and “External Dependencies.”
   • Draw directional arrows showing:
     – How user choice triggers specific build scripts.
     – How build scripts interact with patch sets and options.
     – How CI/CD triggers and monitors the whole process.
   • Consider using color coding and shapes (e.g., rectangles for processes, cylinders for configuration stores, cloud icons for CI/CD) to differentiate component types.
   • Ensure the details capture the essence of a modular, automated script-based build system for patching APKs.

Following these detailed guidelines will ensure that your system design diagram captures all essential architectural elements and clearly conveys the flow from user input to patch generation—and how automated processes tie it all together. This structured and comprehensive diagram will provide an accurate and visually accessible overview of the repository’s architecture to both team members and stakeholders.
</explanation>
